sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-02---Py.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 2 - PyTorch (einops)
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-02---Py.content:
Summary
This is the resource accounting lecture: how to predict, before running anything, how much memory a model needs and how long a computation will take. Percy Liang works bottom-up from tensors and floating point formats through FLOP counting, arithmetic intensity, and roofline analysis, then applies all of it to the memory and compute cost of a training step. einops is introduced along the way as the notation used for tensor operations in the course. The lecture ends with two standard memory-reduction techniques, gradient accumulation and activation checkpointing.
Key Takeaways

Two motivating back-of-the-envelope calculations: training a 70B model on 15T tokens with 1024 H100s at 0.5 MFU takes about 143 days via the 6ND formula; and with AdamW at 2+2+4+4 = 12 bytes per parameter, 8 H100s with 80GB each fit roughly a 53B-parameter model before counting activations.
Precision: fp32 spends 8 bits on the exponent, fp16 only 5, which causes underflow, overflow, and NaNs in training. bf16 keeps fp32’s dynamic range in 16 bits by moving bits from mantissa to exponent, trading resolution that deep learning does not need. Mixed precision uses bf16 for parameters, activations, and gradients with fp32 optimizer state. fp8 is standardized, and nvfp4 gets to 4 bits by scaling per block rather than per value — Nemotron 3 Super was trained in fp4.
FLOPs (work done) and FLOP/s (hardware speed) are distinct, and vendor spec sheets quote the sparsity number, so dense figures are half the headline — about 989 TFLOP/s bf16 for an H100.
A B×D by D×K matmul costs 2·B·D·K FLOPs, which equals 2 × tokens × parameters. The backward pass costs exactly twice the forward pass because it computes gradients both with respect to the input and with respect to the parameters, giving the familiar 6ND total. This approximation holds for transformers as long as the context length is not large enough for the quadratic attention term to dominate.
MFU is actual FLOP/s over spec FLOP/s. About 0.5 is a good result for a real model, a bare matmul might reach 0.8, and 0.1 means something is wrong.
Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved, and it is compared against the accelerator’s own intensity — roughly 295 FLOPs per byte for an H100. ReLU is about 0.25, GELU about 5, a dot product about 0.5, and a matrix-vector product barely above that, so all are memory bound; matrix-matrix multiplication is about n/3 and is compute bound. This is why large matrices and large batches matter: below the accelerator’s intensity, shrinking the work does not make it faster.
The same analysis explains why inference is hard: decoding generates one token at a time, which is a matrix-vector product and therefore memory bound, while training processes a whole sequence at once and stays compute bound.
Training memory breaks down as parameters and gradients at 2 bytes each in bf16, activations at 2·B·D·L, and fp32 optimizer state — 4 bytes per parameter for AdaGrad’s second moments, 8 for Adam’s two moments. Optimizer state is rarely a speed bottleneck but caps the model size that fits.
Gradient accumulation splits a batch into micro-batches and sums gradients before stepping, which keeps activation memory bounded at large effective batch sizes. Activation checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass instead of storing them; checkpointing every √L layers balances √L activation memory against √L recompute overhead.
einops replaces positional indexing with named dimensions: einsum is a generalized matmul where unmentioned dimensions are summed out, reduce generalizes sum/mean/max/min, and rearrange splits or merges dimensions. It removes the transpose bookkeeping that makes backward-pass derivations error-prone, and it is sugar over the same primitives rather than a speedup.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-03---Ar.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 3 - Architectures
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-03---Ar.content:
Summary
Tatsunori Hashimoto surveys modern transformer architectures by comparing what a large number of released models actually do, on the argument that no single paper gives enough detail and the design space is too large to explore directly. The lecture separates choices that have converged across nearly all models — normalization placement, RMSNorm, gated activations, RoPE — from those still in flux, mainly how position and long-range context are handled. It then descends into hyperparameter rules of thumb, training stability tricks, and the attention modifications driven by inference cost. A recurring theme is that architecture is a compromise between expressiveness, hardware efficiency, and not blowing up mid-training, which is why the result looks inelegant. Parallel attention/MLP blocks from GPT-J and PaLM are covered as an idea that has since fallen out of favor.
Key Takeaways

The one thing everyone agrees the original transformer got wrong is normalization placement. Modern models move the norm out of the residual stream (pre-norm), keeping it clean so gradients propagate straight to the output; post-norm changes gradient norms at every block and produces more frequent spikes. The motivation was originally to remove learning-rate warmup, but it stuck for stability and depth. OPT-350M is the odd exception that kept post-norm in the residual stream.
RMSNorm replaces LayerNorm almost everywhere: it drops the mean subtraction and bias, and although LayerNorm is strictly more expressive, there is no measured loss in quality. The reason is arithmetic intensity — normalization is roughly 0.17% of FLOPs but can be up to 25% of runtime because it is memory-movement bound. Bias terms in linear layers are dropped for the same reason.
Gated linear units (SwiGLU in Llama descendants and PaLM, GeGLU in Gemma and T5) are near-universal. Gating adds a third matrix, so the feedforward dimension is scaled by 2/3 to keep the parameter count matched; Shazeer’s parameter-matched comparisons show small but consistent gains. Non-gated models still train fine — GPT-3 used GELU and Nemotron 340B used a squared ReLU.
RoPE encodes position by rotation: split the vector into 2D pairs and rotate each pair by an angle proportional to absolute position, with different frequencies per pair so some capture local and some long-range structure. Inner products then depend only on relative offset. Earlier schemes fail this test — sine/cosine embeddings leak absolute position through cross terms, and additive relative biases (T5, Chinchilla) have no inner-product structure. Rotations are applied to queries and keys at each attention layer. Gemma 4’s p-RoPE rotates only the first coordinates.
Hyperparameters sit in wide, forgiving basins. Feedforward ratio is 4× d_model, or about 2.67 for GLU models after the 2/3 correction (Llama 2 arbitrarily used ~3.5); head_dim × n_heads is kept equal to d_model; the aspect ratio d_model/n_layers is around 100 for nearly every model. Depth is constrained partly by systems concerns — splitting layers means pipeline parallelism, which people avoid, while width splits cleanly with tensor parallelism. Vocabulary is roughly 30k for older monolingual models and 100k–200k for multilingual and production ones. T5’s 64× feedforward multiplier is the great outlier, and T5 v1.1 quietly reverted to about 2.5.
Regularization is counterintuitive here. Single-pass training over more data than compute allows means overfitting is essentially absent, yet weight decay remains common. The evidence is that weight decay acts as an optimization intervention rather than a regularizer: it does not shift the train/validation gap, but combined with learning-rate decay, stronger weight decay runs converge to better minima.
Stability interventions cluster around the two softmaxes. The z-loss penalizes squared log-normalizer to keep the output softmax’s Z near 1 (Devlin 2014, revived by Baichuan, DCLM, OLMo). QK norm applies RMSNorm to queries and keys so the inputs to the attention softmax have consistent scale; it came from multimodal work (Chameleon, Idefics) and is now standard. Logit soft-capping with a tanh (Gemma 2/3/4) is a harder constraint, and NVIDIA’s systematic comparison found it costs quality, while QK norm slightly helps by allowing a higher learning rate.
Attention modifications are driven by inference, not training. During decode the KV cache makes arithmetic intensity roughly n/d + 1/b, which is memory bound and hard to fix for small models. MQA shares one key and value across all heads, multiplying intensity by the head count but losing real expressive power; GQA keeps every query head and only reduces the number of key/value heads, which recovers nearly full quality at much lower inference cost and is why almost all current models use it.
Sliding window attention has been revived for long context: alternate full attention layers with local banded ones, as GPT-3 did and Cohere Command A reintroduced with full attention every fourth layer. Llama 4, Gemma 4, and OLMo 3 all use some version of this; Qwen3.5 uses the same alternating structure but substitutes a gated DeltaNet state space layer for the cheap local layer. Managing the long-context cost/quality tradeoff is where most architecture work is still happening.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-04---At.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 4 - Attention Alternatives
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-04---At.content:
Summary
The second architecture lecture, covering two advanced departures from the vanilla transformer: linear-time alternatives to attention, and mixture of experts. The first half modifies the attention block to escape quadratic dependence on sequence length; the second half modifies the MLP block to add parameters without adding FLOPs. Both are framed as responses to the same pressure — context windows and model sizes are growing faster than compute budgets. The lecture closes by walking through the DeepSeek v1/v2/v3 MoE lineage as a worked example of how these ideas compose in a real model.
Key Takeaways

Feed-forward cost grows linearly with sequence length while attention grows quadratically, so attention overtakes the MLP as the dominant cost at long context; FlashAttention is a constant-factor systems fix (roughly 2x, and it avoids materializing the attention matrix) but does not change the asymptotics.
Linear attention drops the softmax so that matrix multiplication can be reassociated from (QK^T)V to Q(K^TV), changing the cost from n²·d_k to n·d_k·d_v; the reassociated form is algebraically an RNN with a fixed-size state, giving a parallel form for training and a recurrent form for cheap inference. Dropping the softmax is the lossy step; the linear-to-recurrent equivalence after that is exact.
Mamba-2 adds an input-dependent gate that modulates how much state carries forward. Gated DeltaNet adds a second gate controlling whether current information is written at all, plus a delta-rule projector (I − β_t k_t k_t^T) that erases the current key direction before writing — the same update that appears independently in fast-weight programming and test-time training.
The rule of thumb for these recurrences: as long as the gates depend only on the current input and not on the state, the parallel/serial duality survives, which is what makes them trainable at scale.
Every deployed design is a hybrid, not pure linear attention — MiniMax M1 uses 7:1 linear-to-softmax layers, Qwen Next / Qwen 3.5 use 3:1 gated DeltaNet-to-attention. Ablations show little loss at low hybrid ratios and clear degradation on long-context retrieval and QA as the ratio approaches pure RNN.
DeepSeek Sparse Attention (v3.2) takes an orthogonal route: a lightweight indexer scores tokens via ReLU’d qk inner products, top-k selects a small subset, and full attention runs only on that subset. It is still quadratic in the indexer, but the indexer can run in low precision and low dimension, and it is bolted on during long-context extension rather than trained from scratch. GLM adopted the same approach.
MoE replaces one MLP with many, routing each token to top-k experts, so parameters scale while per-token FLOPs stay fixed. Token-choice top-k routing with a simple learned inner-product router is the consensus design; expert choice, hashing, RL/bandit routing, and optimal linear assignment all exist but lost out.
The DeepSeekMoE design — many fine-grained experts plus always-on shared experts that bypass the router — became the standard others copied. OLMoE’s controlled ablations agree that fine-grained experts help but disagree on the value of shared experts.
Training is the hard part: top-k routing is non-differentiable and unchosen experts give no signal, so a rich-get-richer dynamic collapses routing onto a few experts. The fix in practice is not RL or stochastic exploration but an auxiliary load-balancing loss whose gradient pushes down probability mass on popular experts proportional to their token share; removing it sends nearly all tokens to two experts. DeepSeek adds device-level balancing for utilization, and a router z-loss or FP32 router for softmax stability.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-05---GP.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 5 - GPUs, TPUs
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-05---GP.content:
Summary
The opening lecture of the systems portion of the course. It builds a hardware mental model of the GPU, contrasts it with the TPU, then works through the specific tricks that determine whether code saturates the hardware. The organizing question is a plot of matmul throughput against matrix dimension, which has jagged and non-monotonic structure; the lecture is built so that every feature of that plot is explained by the end. It closes by reconstructing FlashAttention from the pieces introduced along the way.
Key Takeaways

Dennard scaling ended in the 2000s, so performance now comes from horizontal parallelism rather than clock speed. A CPU optimizes latency with large control units and few ALUs; a GPU optimizes throughput with hundreds of lightweight cores, and individual tasks may finish slowly while aggregate throughput is high.
The memory hierarchy is the thing to respect: registers and L1/shared memory sit physically on the SM and return in roughly 20-30 cycles, while global memory (HBM) is about an order of magnitude slower. SRAM is not used for everything because it is far more expensive per byte and must be continuously powered.
The execution model is thread (SIMT, all threads in a warp execute the same instruction), block (guaranteed to run on one SM, which is what makes shared memory usable), and warp (32 threads, the scheduling unit). Because threads are swapped in and out at no cost, stalls on memory can be hidden by other warps.
GPUs and TPUs are convergent evolution: every GPU concept maps onto a TPU concept, and a GPU tensor core and a TPU MXU are both systolic arrays. The difference is granularity — many small matmul units on a GPU versus a few very large ones on a TPU, which is why TPUs refuse inputs below a minimum tile dimension. Confusingly, “tensor core” means the matmul unit on a GPU and the whole processor on a TPU.
Since the V100 added tensor cores, matmul has been the one privileged operation, running more than 10x faster than any other floating-point operation — which is why any architecture that scales with compute has a matmul at its core.
Compute throughput is growing faster than memory bandwidth, which in turn grows faster than interconnect bandwidth. That widening gap is why nearly every optimization discussed is a memory optimization, and why the roofline model’s memory-bound diagonal is where badly written code lands.
Six tricks: avoid control divergence (both branches of an if execute, with the inactive threads masked off, so ReLU is written as a multiply by a mask); lower precision; operator fusion; recomputation; memory coalescing; and tiling.
Low precision has become exotic. FP8 has no single format (E4M3 versus E5M2), and MXFP8 attaches a separate E8M0 scale factor to every 32 elements — which breaks transposition, so implementations keep two quantized copies of every matrix. Real speedups are roughly 20-30%, not 2x, because quantization itself costs something, and the last layer is notoriously hard to quantize.
DRAM reads arrive in bursts of roughly 128 bytes, so threads reading down the minor axis of a row-major matrix waste most of each burst; this is why alignment and padding matter, and why Karpathy’s nanoGPT sped up 25% by padding the vocab from 50257 to 50304. Tiling is the highest-impact idea: loading a T×T tile into shared memory cuts global reads by a factor of T. Tile sizing interacts with SM count — at 1792 a matmul produces 98 tiles which fit in the A100’s 108 SMs, while 1793 produces 120 tiles and forces a second, mostly idle wave (wave quantization).
FlashAttention is exactly these pieces combined: tiled matmuls, an online softmax that carries a running maximum and rescales when a larger value appears, fusion of the whole sequence into one kernel, and recomputation of the N² activations on the backward pass instead of storing them.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-06---Ke.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 6 - Kernels, Triton, XLA
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-06---Ke.content:
Summary
A hands-on continuation of the GPU lecture, moving from hardware concepts to actual kernel code. It covers the places where the clean programming model leaks and hardware details decide performance, then argues for measuring before optimizing, then writes Triton kernels of increasing difficulty ending at a tiled matmul. The through-line is that the programming model is simple enough to learn quickly, but performance is governed by warps, banks, cache lines, and occupancy, none of which appear in the model itself.
Key Takeaways

The programming model is threads, thread blocks (CTAs), and a grid of blocks; the reason blocks exist at all is shared memory, which is what lets non-elementwise operations like softmax and matmul avoid round-tripping through HBM.
Warps are 32 threads executing in lockstep, so branching serializes both sides. Less obviously, a warp scheduler switches between resident warps at zero cost, which is how the hardware hides the long latency of an HBM read — a stalled warp is simply replaced by one that can compute.
Occupancy is a budget calculation, not a goal. A thread may use at most 255 registers, and registers per SM are fixed, so 128 threads per block at 160 registers each allows only 3 blocks per SM, which is 12 of a possible 64 warps — 18% occupancy. Low occupancy is not automatically bad if each thread does more work, which is the idea behind thread coarsening.
Shared memory is split into 32 banks of 4 bytes, and only one thread may hit a bank per cycle, so 32 threads reading down a column serialize into a 32-way bank conflict. This is unavoidable in matmul, where one operand must be read by rows and the other by columns; swizzling the shared-memory layout is the standard fix. Bank conflicts (shared memory) and coalescing (128-byte HBM cache lines) are separate constraints that look superficially similar.
Blocks are scheduled onto a finite number of SMs, so launching 160 blocks on 148 SMs leaves a second wave of 12 blocks with most of the chip idle; the fix is changing block size rather than hoping the scheduler compensates.
The recommended loop is benchmark, change, benchmark again. Benchmarking correctly means warming up first (to exclude lazy compilation), timing with CUDA events, synchronizing because GPU execution is asynchronous, and averaging over repeats. Matmul wall time is roughly flat until around 2000 dimensions, because smaller matrices cannot fill the hardware.
Profiling shows what actually ran. A hand-written PyTorch GeLU dispatches a separate kernel per graph primitive, each reading and writing HBM; the built-in GeLU is one hand-written CUDA kernel; torch.compile fuses the naive version into a single generated Triton kernel. Kernel names are informative — a CUTLASS name encodes the architecture (SM100 is Blackwell) and the tile shape, and changing matrix dimensions selects a different kernel.
Triton is written in Python at thread-block granularity: compute a program ID, derive offsets with tl.arange, build a mask for the ragged final block, tl.load from pointers, compute as if on tensors, and tl.store back. It compiles to PTX, which is per-thread and reveals decisions the programmer never made — including thread coarsening, where one thread was given eight elements because it was too light.
The examples escalate in exactly the way the hardware forces: GeLU is elementwise and needs no coordination; softmax assigns one row per block so no cross-block communication is needed; row-sum introduces tiling with a per-thread accumulator once a row exceeds the block size; and matmul is the canonical case, where the naive version does O(MKN) reads for constant arithmetic intensity, loading everything into shared memory would give O(N) but does not fit, and tiling reaches arithmetic intensity on the order of the tile size. Fusing an elementwise activation before the final store is free once the kernel is already written.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-07---Pa.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 7 - Parallelism
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-07---Pa.content:
Summary
The first of two parallelism lectures, taught by Percy Liang, introducing the mechanics of multi-GPU training from the ground up. It extends the previous week’s single-GPU kernel material by adding two more levels to the memory hierarchy: intra-node GPUs connected by NVLink/NVSwitch, and inter-node GPUs connected by InfiniBand or Ethernet. The first half covers collective communication primitives and the hardware and software stack that implements them (NCCL, torch.distributed); the second half implements data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism on a multi-layer MLP. It deliberately works at the level of explicit collective calls rather than library wrappers, since the course builds things from scratch.
Key Takeaways

The framing principle is the same as for single-GPU work: compute is far from data, so the job is to orchestrate computation to avoid data-transfer bottlenecks. What counted as slow last week (HBM) counts as fast here.
Two distinct reasons to go multi-GPU: parameters, gradients, and optimizer state do not fit in one device’s HBM (a B200 has 192 GB, far short of a 1T-parameter model), and splitting work across devices trains faster even when the model does fit.
Collectives divide into warm-ups (broadcast, scatter, gather, reduce) and the ones that actually drive LM training (all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce), plus all-to-all, which matters for MoE routing where each rank holds both a data shard and a subset of experts.
The key identity, demonstrated by example in code: all-reduce equals reduce-scatter followed by all-gather. Breaking all-reduce into its two halves is what later enables ZeRO and FSDP to intervene between the steps.
Hardware calibration: typically 8 GPUs per node on NVLink/NVSwitch, with NVLink 5 giving about 1.8 TB/s aggregate against roughly 8 TB/s of B200 HBM bandwidth, so inter-GPU transfer is about 4x slower than local memory. NVL72 extends a single NVLink domain to 72 GPUs.
RDMA lets one GPU read and write another’s memory without involving the CPU. NVLink/NVSwitch and InfiniBand support it; plain Ethernet does not, which is why RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) exists as a cheaper alternative to InfiniBand.
Measured effective bandwidth for all-reduce works out to size * 2 * (world_size - 1) / world_size / duration, about 400 GB/s in the demo. As world size grows the factor approaches 1, so bandwidth is independent of both world size and the ring/tree topology NCCL chooses. All-reduce moves twice the data of reduce-scatter and takes twice as long, so the two report the same bandwidth.
DDP is a one-line change to a normal training loop: after the backward pass, all-reduce and average param.grad across ranks, so every rank updates identical parameters from a distinct data shard. It is fully modular and does not care what the forward pass looks like.
Tensor parallelism (here column-parallel) instead splits each weight matrix, so every layer must all-gather activations in the forward pass and reduce-scatter in the backward pass — a duality that recurs throughout. Pipeline parallelism splits layers and uses point-to-point send/recv, with micro-batches to shrink pipeline bubbles.
Choice of strategy follows the interconnect: tensor parallelism moves large activations every layer and so belongs inside an NVLink domain, while pipeline parallelism tolerates slow links and is used in decentralized training. Data parallelism is bounded by the critical batch size, beyond which more batch stops helping.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-08---Pa.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 8 - Parallelism
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-08---Pa.content:
Summary
The second parallelism lecture, taught by Tatsunori Hashimoto, moving from the mechanics of the previous lecture to the full modern toolbox and how practitioners combine it. It works through the ZeRO stages and FSDP, then pipeline, tensor, sequence, expert, and context parallelism, with careful memory accounting at each step. The recurring theme is that no single strategy dominates: each consumes a different resource (batch size, bandwidth, memory) and each has a regime where it fails. It ends with a simple prescription for combining them into so-called 4D parallelism, and a survey of published parallelism configurations from real training runs.
Key Takeaways

Memory accounting motivates everything: a rule of thumb of roughly five copies of weights and about 16 bytes per parameter, with Adam’s first and second moments dominating. Naive data parallelism replicates all of that on every device and saves no memory at all.
ZeRO stage 1 shards optimizer state, replacing DDP’s single all-reduce with a reduce-scatter of gradients plus an all-gather of updated parameters. Since those two equal one all-reduce, the memory saving is communication-free.
ZeRO stage 2 shards gradients by reducing each layer’s gradients as the backward sweep produces them and freeing them immediately, which is again free. ZeRO stage 3 (FSDP) shards parameters too, gathering them on demand per layer: two all-gathers plus one reduce-scatter, so one extra all-gather, hidden in practice by overlapping communication with computation.
The practical payoff: on 8x A100 the baseline cannot fit a 7B model, while ZeRO stage 3 reaches roughly 50B. FSDP’s utilization lands close to single-GPU performance.
Data parallelism consumes the global batch size as a resource, and the critical batch size caps how far that goes — the reason model parallelism becomes necessary rather than optional. ZeRO also leaves activation memory untouched.
Model parallelism differs from FSDP in what moves: FSDP ships parameters and runs the ordinary computation, while pipeline, tensor, and expert parallelism ship activations.
Pipeline parallelism’s utilization is stages over micro-batches, so bubbles shrink only with large batches. Zero-bubble pipelining splits the backward pass into propagating partials (urgent, blocks the next stage) and computing weight gradients (deferrable into gaps), nearly filling the pipeline. Its communication is only b*s*h and point-to-point, so it belongs on the slowest links.
Tensor parallelism cuts column-wise at MLP up-projections and attention projections and row-wise at the corresponding outputs, replicating small ops like layer norms and routers. It all-reduces at activation size every matmul, so it stays within one box (up to 8 on GPUs); TPUs can go wider because of the uniform mesh.
Activation memory is about 34*s*b*h plus a quadratic attention term. Tensor parallelism divides 24 of the 34 but leaves roughly 10*s*b*h in layer norms, dropout, and residual inputs; sequence parallelism splits that remainder along the sequence axis with all-gathers and reduce-scatters, and recomputation removes the softmax term, giving a practical floor of 34*s*b*h/t.
For MoEs, expert parallelism is preferred over tensor parallelism (per NVIDIA’s Megatron guidance), since slicing matrices too finely shrinks matmuls and hurts utilization. Its all-to-all dispatch is latency-critical, which is why DeepSeek’s DeepEP library reaches for undocumented PTX instructions.
The prescription: shard the model until it fits, using tensor or expert parallelism inside the fast interconnect, then pipeline or ZeRO-3 to close the gap, then spend remaining devices on data parallelism, with gradient accumulation if the batch gets too small.
Published configurations bear this out: OLMo 7B trained purely with FSDP; DeepSeek V3 uses 64-way expert parallelism across 8-machine groups; Llama 3 405B ran TP 8, CP 1, PP 16, DP 128, raising context parallelism for long-context extension (and hit 148 GPU failures); Gemma 2 uses FSDP with tensor and sequence parallelism and no pipeline at all.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-09---Sc.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 9 - Scaling Laws
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-09---Sc.content:
Summary
The first of two scaling-law lectures, taught by Tatsunori Hashimoto, covering the basics before a later advanced session on muP and optimizers. The framing problem is practical: given one very expensive training run, how do you make architecture, data, batch size, and learning rate decisions from small-scale experiments instead of guessing or copying? It connects scaling laws to classical statistical rates, works through data scaling, then scaling as a tool for engineering decisions, and closes with a detailed post-mortem of the Kaplan/Chinchilla disagreement as a lesson in how fragile these fits are.
Key Takeaways

Scaling laws long predate modern LLMs: Cortes and Vapnik at Bell Labs fitted error-decay curves in 1993, Banko and Brill and Kolachina et al. found power laws for data in NLP, and Hestness et al. in 2017 established polynomial trends across speech, translation, and language modeling, including emergence and the compute-scaling implication.
A straight line on a log-log plot means polynomial decay and, usually, that you are far from the asymptote. Mean estimation gives error sigma squared over n and hence slope -1; fitted neural exponents are around -0.1 to -0.3, far slower, consistent with a nonparametric rate of roughly n to the -1/d, i.e. models behaving like nonparametric smoothers in about 10 dimensions (an argument pushed further by Bahri et al., with caveats about intrinsic-dimension estimators).
Across many interventions the slope stays put and only the intercept moves — true for SGD versus Adam, for regularization and ensembling, and for data mixtures. The practical consequence is that the best data mix at small scale stays best at large scale, so people often skip the scaling law and just pick the winner from small runs.
Repeating data costs nothing up to roughly four epochs under standard recipes; past that the realized curve falls away from what fresh data would have given. Data filtering is scale-dependent in the same spirit: more compute means looser filters, since you would rather add mediocre data than repeat good data.
Architecture and optimizer choices can be settled by comparing curves rather than by training giant models. Tay et al.’s T5-scale study anticipated what frontier models actually adopted — gated linear units and switch-style sparsity scale well, efficient-attention variants like Performer do not.
Not all parameters count equally. Kaplan et al. excluded embedding parameters to get clean curves and also excluded the final softmax layer, a decision that materially changed the resulting law. Predictable scaling is engineered, not automatic: it depends on choosing the right x-axis and tuning hyperparameters properly.
The critical batch size marks the crossover from a variance-limited regime, where each extra example reduces gradient noise with near-perfect returns, to a bias-limited one. It is estimated by fitting the tradeoff between steps and examples to a target loss, giving B_crit as minimum examples over minimum steps, and it grows predictably as the target loss falls (McCandlish et al.).
Learning rate has two competing schools: predict how the optimum shifts (roughly 1/width) and extrapolate it, or reparameterize with muP so the optimum stays fixed across scales. Both have been used successfully at frontier scale.
Upstream perplexity and downstream benchmarks can diverge badly — in one architecture comparison the best-perplexity model was not the best downstream model. Fit scaling laws on perplexity because it is clean and low-variance, but treat transfer as a separate, less certain claim.
Chinchilla offered three fitting methods (lower envelope, IsoFLOP, and parametric surface fitting) that agreed on roughly equal exponents and 20 tokens per parameter, against Kaplan’s 0.73/0.27 split that drove the era of giant under-trained models. The “Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling” paper showed the gap comes from a chain of small choices — parameter counting, learning-rate warmup, and a fixed suboptimal batch size — and Epoch AI’s refit showed Chinchilla’s own method 3 only disagreed because of underfitting.
The 20:1 ratio is not the target for production models: most compute goes to R&D and serving, so deliberately overtraining smaller models is the right tradeoff. IsoFLOP sweeps remain the durable default tool for any such decision.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-10---In.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 10 - Inference
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-10---In.content:
Summary
A one-lecture treatment of inference, placed between the two scaling-law lectures. It argues that inference is a fundamentally different workload from training because autoregressive generation cannot parallelize over the sequence dimension, then works through the arithmetic intensity of the MLP and attention layers to show exactly where the bottleneck sits. The second half is a survey of ways to make inference faster: shrinking the KV cache through architecture changes, quantization, pruning and distillation, lossless speculative decoding, and serving-system techniques for dynamic workloads. The framing throughout is that inference is memory-bound, so almost every technique reduces to moving fewer bytes without losing accuracy.
Key Takeaways

Training is a one-time cost but inference is a repeated one: OpenAI is estimated to produce around 8.6 trillion tokens a day, so in under four days it generates as many tokens as DeepSeek-V4 was trained on (32 trillion). With agents, most generated tokens are never read by a human, so token count is effectively compute spend and there is no point at which “fast enough” saturates.
Three metrics that trade off: time to first token (essentially prefill time), latency (tokens per second for one query), and throughput (tokens per second across all queries). Batch size moves latency and throughput in opposite directions.
The core asymmetry: in training the sequence is just another tensor dimension, but generation produces one token at a time, so arithmetic intensity stays low. MLP intensity is roughly B·T, which makes prefill compute-bound and generation acceptable given enough concurrent requests; attention during generation has intensity below 1, versus the roughly 295 an H100 needs to be compute-bound.
Attention is the fundamental bottleneck because every sequence has its own KV cache, so increasing batch size does not amortize anything — unlike MLP weights, which are loaded once and shared across the batch.
KV cache reduction is the main lever, since memory is the constraint: grouped-query attention shrinks the cache by N/K; DeepSeek’s multi-head latent attention compresses activations into a smaller latent (16k to 512 in DeepSeek-V2) and materializes K and V on demand, needing extra dimensions because it is incompatible with RoPE; cross-layer attention shares KV across layers; sliding-window attention makes the cache independent of sequence length but costs accuracy, so practical models interleave local and full-attention layers.
Quantization-aware training simulates quantization error in the forward pass but needs expensive large-scale training, so post-training quantization is more common: GPTQ quantizes layer by layer using Hessian information and propagates the error into the not-yet-quantized weights, while activation-aware methods spend higher precision on the weights that interact with large activation channels.
Pruning estimates unit and layer importance from activation magnitudes on a calibration set, removes parts of the model, then post-trains to heal it; an NVIDIA result took a 15B model down to 8B at modest accuracy cost and far less compute than training from scratch.
Speculative decoding is lossless, not approximate: a cheap draft model proposes K tokens, the target model scores them in one parallel pass, and each is accepted with probability min(1, q/p), otherwise a token is drawn from the residual distribution. This is rejection sampling that always yields a sample, and the sweet spot is around three or four draft tokens — too few wastes the target model’s batching, too many get rejected.
Serving under dynamic load: continuous batching (Orca) adds arriving requests to the batch and evicts finished ones each decode step, selective batching concatenates variable-length sequences for the MLP layers where attention cannot be shared, and PagedAttention (vLLM) stores the KV cache in non-contiguous blocks to kill internal and external fragmentation, which also allows shared system prompts and copy-on-write prefix sharing across samples.
Closing argument: the transformer’s KV cache makes it inherently inference-unfriendly, so architectures designed for inference (state space models, linear attention, diffusion) may hold the largest remaining gains.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-11---Sc.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 11 - Scaling Laws
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-11---Sc.content:
Summary
The second scaling lecture, deliberately a grab bag of the practical details that come after the classical Kaplan and Chinchilla material covered earlier in the course. It is organised around two contrasting real recipes — MiniCPM, which uses muP to make the optimal learning rate scale-invariant, and DeepSeek LLM, which instead fits scaling laws to predict the optimal learning rate and batch size — and then generalises each into its own section. The middle of the lecture surveys how recent open-weight releases (Qwen, Kimi K2, Hunyuan, LLaMA 3, MiniMax-01) actually use scaling experiments, and covers optimizers including Muon. The last third is a derivation of muP from two invariants, followed by its known failure cases. The recurring message is that extrapolating from small-scale experiments remains partly an art.
Key Takeaways

Two opposing strategies for scale-sensitive hyperparameters: stabilize them so the optimum does not move (MiniCPM’s muP approach), or accept that they move and fit a scaling law that predicts where the optimum will be (the DeepSeek approach). Both are in use.
MiniCPM’s muP recipe scales the embedding output, the residual connections by the square root of the number of layers, the initialization of matrix-shaped tensors by the fan-in/fan-out ratio, the per-tensor learning rates, and the LM head. The result is clean: the loss minimum sits at roughly 1e-2 across model sizes, removing the need to tune learning rate at the target scale.
Warmup-stable-decay learning rate: a fixed-step warmup, a long constant phase, and a rapid decay over the last 10-20% down to roughly 10% of peak. Its point is reusability — cosine requires knowing the token horizon in advance, so every data-scaling point needs a fresh run, whereas WSD lets you rewind to the last stable checkpoint and re-decay. WSD curves look like they are losing until the decay phase reclaims the gains, and end up comparable to a well-tuned cosine.
DeepSeek grid-searches learning rate and batch size at many scales and fits both against non-embedding FLOPs. The batch size fit is a convincing line; the learning rate fit is noisier, and grid quantization error is a real weakness of this approach. Their extrapolated predictions for the final large runs land close to the actual results.
The StepFun hyperparameter study finds the loss surface over (learning rate, batch size) is smooth and convex along each slice, which is what makes gridding viable at all. Its headline claim is that optimal batch size depends mainly on total data, roughly as its square root, while optimal learning rate falls with model size and rises with data — the latter is counterintuitive and contested. Under Chinchilla-style scaling the two effects partly cancel, recovering a DeepSeek-like law where learning rate falls with compute.
These fitted laws transfer to MoEs reasonably well once active parameters are controlled for, but shift with the training data distribution, so the specific constants are contingent on the data rather than universal.
MoE-specific scaling laws are the current frontier item: Kimi K2 sweeps sparsity against loss and picks a sparsity of 48 where returns diminish, Hunyuan runs the same style of analysis and lands on about 96 tokens per active parameter, LLaMA 3 fits a sigmoid mapping log loss to downstream benchmark accuracy, and MiniMax-01 uses scaling curves to show lightning (linear), softmax and hybrid attention are comparable, which is how they justified shipping the hybrid.
Muon treats matrix-shaped parameters differently from vector ones: after the momentum step it orthogonalizes the update via Newton-Schulz, effectively setting every singular value to 1, which is the spectral-norm analogue of Adam’s per-coordinate normalization. Newton-Schulz is used because it needs only matrix multiplies, unlike an SVD, which is slow on GPUs; vector parameters still use AdamW. It wins big on the NanoGPT speedrun, controlled studies show the gain shrinking as scale grows, and yet Kimi K2 was trained entirely with it — with no published ablation at that scale.
Optimizer comparisons are badly confounded. An undertuned Adam baseline or a non-optimal weight decay can manufacture or erase the entire gain, and most papers vary model size but neglect the Chinchilla token-to-parameter ratio, which is a second scaling axis that some algorithms are sensitive to. A Marin example shows a beautiful scaling trend holding for orders of magnitude and then blowing up.
The muP derivation asserts two invariants as width grows: activations at initialization stay the same scale, and one gradient step changes activations by O(1) (feature learning, as opposed to the neural tangent kernel regime where that change vanishes). Tracking orders of magnitude through a deep linear network yields the initialization scale and a per-layer learning rate of fan-out over fan-in for SGD, or one over fan-in for Adam. Stress testing shows muP survives SwiGLU and most architecture variation but breaks with a learned RMSNorm gain, sign-based optimizers such as Lion, and large decoupled weight decay.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-12---Ev.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 12 - Evaluation
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-12---Ev.content:
Summary
The lecture that bridges modelling and data, on the grounds that you cannot choose training data without first deciding what behaviour you want. It frames evaluation as the problem of turning an abstract construct such as “reasoning” into a concrete metric, and argues this matters because benchmarks set the North Star that shapes what gets built. It then walks through the families of evaluation in turn — perplexity, exams, chat, agentic, pure reasoning, and safety — before turning to cross-cutting problems: ecological validity, train-test contamination, and benchmark quality. The conclusion is that there is no single correct evaluation, only evaluations chosen deliberately for a stated purpose.
Key Takeaways

Perplexity is the natural metric because a language model is a distribution, and the argument for it is that its unique minimizer is the true distribution, so pushing it down far enough gets you everything else. It drove language modelling research through the 2010s on in-distribution splits (Penn Treebank, WikiText-103, One Billion Word) until GPT-2 shifted the norm to zero-shot out-of-distribution evaluation on standard benchmarks.
Perplexity’s weakness is that it charges for every token equally, including uninformative ones, which conditional perplexity partly fixes by scoring only the continuation after a prompt. Several accuracy benchmarks are perplexity in disguise — LAMBADA is fill-in-the-blank chosen so resolution requires long-range context, and HellaSwag is multiple-choice sentence completion.
A perplexity leaderboard has a trust problem that downstream benchmarks do not: you must believe the submitted probabilities are a normalized distribution, whereas a black-box model can simply be prompted and scored.
Exam benchmarks run on a saturation treadmill. MMLU (57 subjects, evaluated few-shot on GPT-3, at which point barely above chance for small models) is now around 90; MMLU-Pro added chain of thought and ten choices, dropping accuracy to 33 before it climbed back near 90; GPQA used 61 PhD contractors with expert validation and a DIAMOND subset, where PhD experts themselves score about 65% and GPT-4 scored 39%, now around 94; Humanity’s Last Exam keeps a private held-out split and still has headroom.
Exams do not capture real usage. Chat evaluation instead uses Chatbot Arena’s anonymized pairwise preferences fitted to Elo ratings, which works from a sparse comparison graph and absorbs new models and prompts naturally, but conflates style with correctness, draws on an unknown rater population, and rewards sycophancy. AlpacaEval replaces humans with LLM-as-judge win rate against a baseline, originally biased toward long answers until a length-debiasing regression was added, and correlates 0.98 with Chatbot Arena. WildBench adds a per-prompt checklist so the judging task is well defined at all.
Agentic benchmarks evaluate what a model does rather than what it says, and they measure the scaffold as much as the model — the same model with different scaffolds scores differently. Examples: SWE-bench (resolve a GitHub issue, graded by unit tests, roughly 16% in 2024 and now above 90 on the Verified split), Terminal-Bench (crowdsourced terminal tasks, 89 of them in 2.0), CyBench (40 capture-the-flag tasks, about 10% at release and now essentially solved), and Kaggle-style ML engineering benchmarks.
Effective agent scaffolds converge on explicit planning with a to-do list rather than stream-of-consciousness chain of thought, hierarchical delegation to sub-agents that return only results so the main context stays clean, and reading and writing memory to files once the context window is exceeded.
ARC-AGI tries to isolate fluid reasoning from world knowledge, with tasks designed to be fully solvable by humans and useless to memorize. Pre-trained models scored essentially zero, exactly as intended, until the o1 and o3 reasoning models broke it open; ARC-AGI-2 is close to solved and the interactive ARC-AGI-3 currently scores very low.
Safety has no agreed definition: HarmBench tests refusal of harmful prompts, AIR-Bench builds a risk taxonomy from EU, China and US regulation plus company policies, and GCG shows that jailbreak strings optimized against open models transfer. The lecture stresses that safety is contextual across jurisdictions, that risks differ in kind (hallucination, sycophancy, deskilling, inequality) with some anti-correlated with capability and others correlated, and that capabilities like cybersecurity are dual use.
Contamination cannot be ruled out for internet-scale training, and is usually indirect rather than literal test-set training. Mitigations: infer contamination from benchmark question-order preference, push norms requiring providers to report overlap alongside claimed scores, build fresh evals past the model cutoff (LiveCodeBench, UncheatableEval — though timestamps are not fully safe since new uploads can be derived from old material), or use private evals such as internal code or unpublished personal writing, which suit perplexity well.
Benchmark quality is a real failure mode: SWE-bench Verified exists because the original tasks had inadequate unit tests, audits of GSM8K and MMLU found unanswerable items, and one agentic benchmark awarded 38% to an agent returning an empty response. Tools such as Docent inspect agent traces, and the standing advice is to read actual model outputs to confirm the benchmark measures what you think it measures.
There is no one true evaluation — the right choice depends on whether you are making a purchase decision, proxying intelligence for research, informing policy, or getting developer feedback. Before foundation models research evaluated methods against fixed splits; now it mostly evaluates end models and systems, with exceptions like the NanoGPT speedrun that deliberately evaluate a training algorithm.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-13---Da.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 13 - Data (Sources, Datasets)
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-13---Da.content:
Summary
First of two data lectures, covering where pre-training data comes from and which datasets the field has actually used. The first half is about access: what “trained on the internet” really means, how crawling works, and what technical and legal restrictions (robots.txt, terms of service, copyright, fair use) govern what can be collected. The second half is a chronological tour of pre-training corpora from BERT and GPT-2 through C4, The Pile, RefinedWeb, FineWeb, Dolma, DCLM, Nemotron, The Stack, and Common Pile, tracking how filtering strategy evolved from hand-written rules to model-based classifiers. It follows the evaluation lecture and sets up Lecture 14, which covers the processing pipeline itself.
Key Takeaways

Model developers disclose architecture and training procedure but not data, for two reasons: data is the competitive differentiator, and naming your sources invites copyright liability. Llama 3’s paper is the canonical example.
The trainable web is much smaller than the web. Dynamic app content and the deep web are not reachable by link-following crawlers, walled gardens (Facebook, X, LinkedIn, NYT) require authentication, and Longpre’s “Consent in Crisis” found robots.txt full-restriction rates jumping toward ~50% after mid-2023.
Copyright covers expression, not ideas, requires no registration, and lasts 75 years; so essentially all web content is copyrighted, and lawful use runs through either a license (Creative Commons, or a paid deal) or a fair-use argument under the four Section 107 factors.
Recent rulings split training from acquisition: training was held to be fair use in the Anthropic and Meta cases, but pirating books was not — Anthropic settled for $1.5B, roughly $3,000 a book, even though buying and scanning the same books would have been fine.
Common Crawl releases WARC (raw HTTP responses) and WET (pre-extracted text) files; the DataComp-LM ablation shows that running your own extraction with trafilatura or resiliparse beats using WET, so the HTML-to-text step measurably affects model quality.
High-value sources are distributed rather than crawled: Wikipedia and Stack Exchange publish periodic dumps, GitHub repos come over the git protocol with metadata via GitHub Archive’s hourly event stream, and arXiv offers bulk download with clear Creative Commons licensing.
Quality filtering evolved through three ideas: proxy signals for quality (GPT-2’s Reddit outbound links with >3 karma), hand-written rules (C4’s punctuation/sentence-count/bad-word rules, which also stripped curly braces and therefore code), and trained classifiers (GPT-3, then DCLM’s fastText model using OpenHermes and ELI5 as positives against RefinedWeb negatives).
Scale numbers show how aggressive filtering has become: DCLM-pool holds 240T unfiltered tokens and the released set keeps about 1.4% of it, while Nemotron argued DCLM over-filters and used LLM-scored educational value plus synthetic rephrasing to reach 6T tokens.
Shadow-library data caused lasting damage: Books3, distributed via The Pile and used by Llama 1, traced back to Bibliotik and has since been stripped from derivatives like RedPajama V1 — one reason labs stopped describing their data at all.
Common Pile tested the strict-licensing path, assembling 8TB of permissively licensed text and finding license laundering and collection-level licenses that don’t cover individual works; the resulting models beat 2023-era models but not contemporary Qwen.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-14---Da.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 14 - Data
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-14---Da.content:
Summary
Second of two data lectures, covering the processing pipeline rather than the sources. It walks the four stages applied to raw data after collection — transformation (HTML and PDF to text), filtering, deduplication, and mixing — and closes with a survey of recent post-training data efforts, mostly for code and agentic software engineering. The deduplication section is the most technical part of the pair, deriving MinHash and locality-sensitive hashing from scratch. Where Lecture 13 asked what data exists and whether it can be used, this lecture asks how to turn it into a training set.
Key Takeaways

Filtering has one general shape: given a small high-quality target set and a large raw pool, fit a cheap scorer and keep the raw documents that look like the target. Generative scorers use KenLM n-gram perplexity; discriminative ones use fastText linear classifiers, which is now the default.
The same machinery serves different goals by swapping the target set: fastText language ID across 176 languages, math data via OpenMathText (LaTeX rules, KenLM trained on ProofPile, plus a math classifier with a lower bar for documents containing LaTeX), toxicity via Jigsaw Toxic Comments, and educational value via phi-1’s trick of labelling 100k documents with GPT-4 and distilling that into a cheap Random Forest.
There is no universal quality threshold, because the optimum depends on the token budget: filtered data wins early, but once you epoch over a small high-quality pool you overfit, and training longer on unfiltered data ends up ahead.
Deduplication matters for compute, memorization, and contamination alike; an audit of C4 found one gas-mask product description repeated 61,000 times, and near-duplicates from mirrors, forks, licenses, boilerplate, and templated spam are pervasive.
Pairwise comparison is quadratic, so dedup relies on hashing: MinHash is built so the probability of a hash collision equals the Jaccard similarity of two sets, turning a similarity question into a linear-time one.
Locality-sensitive hashing sharpens that stochastic signal into a near-threshold decision by splitting n hash functions into b bands of r and declaring a match if any band matches entirely; the transition sits near (1/b)^(1/r), raising r shifts it right and raising b shifts it left, and the collision probability at the threshold is about 0.64.
Mixing weights must account for source size, not just quality: with 10T low-quality and 10B high-quality tokens, a uniform mixture trained for 1T tokens touches 5% of the low-quality pool once while epoching the high-quality pool 50 times. UniMax addresses this with a hard per-source epoch cap.
Regression-based methods (RegMix, Olmix) train a swarm of small proxy models on sampled Dirichlet mixtures, fit a log-linear map from mixture weights to loss, and optimize it — but the optimizer pushes toward extremes the regression never saw, and targeting downstream evals quietly overfits the pre-training mix to those evals.
Simulated epoching keeps the small-scale proxy honest by downsampling every source in proportion to the scale gap (1 in 100 for a 10B proxy versus a 1T run), so the proxy experiences the same data scarcity the full run will.
Open post-training data is now overwhelmingly synthetic and increasingly agentic: OpenThoughts found a few sources beat many and that QwQ-32B was a better teacher than the stronger DeepSeek-R1, while SWE-Zero exploited the fact that models solve nearly 70% of SWE tasks without execution feedback to skip per-repo Docker environments and collect 300k trajectories, an approach SWE-rebench scaled to 12M.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-15---Mi.filePath: sources/Stanford CS336 - Lecture 15 - Mid and Post-Training.md
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-15---Mi.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 15 - Mid/Post-Training
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-15---Mi.content:
Summary
The first of two post-training lectures, covering the path from a GPT-3-style base model to something close to ChatGPT; the next lecture covers the step from there to reasoning models. It splits into supervised fine-tuning and RLHF, and in both halves the emphasis is on data rather than algorithms — the lecturer notes that frontier post-training details are now trade secrets, so the best public references (the summarization-from-human-feedback appendices, Anthropic’s HH paper, the InstructGPT appendix) predate the competitive era. The algorithmic content covers PPO briefly and derives DPO, and the lecture ends on over-optimization and mode collapse.
Key Takeaways

SFT data evolved away from FLAN’s premise that post-training needs pre-training-like scale: FLAN built instructions out of existing NLP benchmarks, inheriting unnatural formats and even hallucinated summaries, and the field later found that a strong base model needs relatively few high-quality examples.
Style and capability move independently. Annotators reliably prefer longer, bullet-pointed answers, so some SFT sets shift AlpacaEval win rates without moving standard benchmarks — engagement signals can improve while the model gets no smarter.
Training on correct but unknown-to-the-model facts can be actively harmful: an SFT example containing a citation teaches both the fact and the habit of emitting citations, and the habit generalizes into hallucinated references. Schulman’s argument is that calibration is policy-dependent, which is a reason to use RL rather than more SFT.
Safety tuning trades violation rate against false-refusal rate (refusing “how do I kill a Python process”); Tulu 3 uses roughly 50k safety examples mined from WildChat jailbreak attempts, and even ~500 examples sharply reduce unsafe compliance, though fine-grained policy distinctions still need large-scale collection.
Instruction data is now mixed into the decay phase of pre-training, which is why “base model” has become a misleading label — models described as base are often already trained on UltraChat and similar sets. Mid-training is short enough that mixture ablations run there are used to set the pre-training mix.
Pre-training and SFT are generative modeling (fit a distribution); RLHF is reward maximization, where collapsing to a single response per prompt is acceptable if the reward is good. That distinction explains the diversity loss seen after RLHF.
Annotation has bifurcated: a Scale platform sample is roughly 70% bachelor’s or master’s holders at a modal age of 35, bespoke domain experts earn median wages above $50/hour and sometimes above $100/hour, and low-cost annotation still exists underneath. Verifying that annotators are not themselves using ChatGPT is now a core difficulty.
Annotator composition shapes model behavior measurably: post-trained models shifted from Protestant and Roman Catholic opinion profiles toward Buddhist, Hindu, and atheist ones, matching the InstructGPT annotator demographics, and Hosking et al. found non-experts over-weight formatting while experts weight factuality.
Model-based annotation won on cost and quality for anyone not at the frontier — Zephyr deliberately tried paid human collection, found it slower, costlier, and no better, and fell back to AI feedback; UltraChat, UltraFeedback, and Tulu 3 are now the standard pattern.
DPO drops both the reward model and on-policy sampling: assuming a nonparametric policy, the KL-regularized optimum is the reference policy exponentially tilted by reward, so inverting for the implied reward yields a loss that raises the winner’s log-probability and lowers the loser’s, scaled by how wrong the implied reward model was. Llama used SFT, DPO, then rejection sampling in an outer loop.
The main RLHF failure modes are over-optimizing a learned reward model, which makes the KL term load-bearing, and mode collapse; OpenAI’s own GPT-4 material shows RLHF leaves models uncalibrated, which matters for the exploration needed in RLVR.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-16---Po.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 16 - Post-Training - RLVR
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-16---Po.content:
Summary
The second post-training lecture, covering reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) and the thinking models it produces. It picks up from the previous lecture’s downbeat conclusion that RLHF is capped by reward-model overoptimization, and argues that verifiable domains such as math and code let you pour in compute the way AlphaGo could. The first half develops the algorithms — PPO, why people want to escape it, and GRPO — and the second half reads recent open-source technical reports (DeepSeek R1, Kimi K1.5, Qwen 3, Qwen3-Coder-Next) to show how those algorithms appear in practice. The recurring theme is that RLVR is only as good as the reward it optimizes.
Key Takeaways

RLHF is annotation-bottlenecked: you train a reward model on preference data and eventually overfit it no matter how you regularize. AlphaGo-style domains work because the win/loss condition is exactly the objective, so compute can be added indefinitely; math and code are attractive because they are closer to that regime.
PPO is disfavored less for theory than for engineering. It needs a value model as large as the policy, which consumes memory wanted for inference; it is notoriously implementation-sensitive (the “37 implementation details” problem); KL terms operate token by token; and practitioners commonly set gamma = lambda = 1 in the generalized advantage estimator, which degenerates it back to a bandit problem and discards the structure PPO was supposed to provide.
DPO is the wrong tool here: it is a specific solution for pairwise Bradley-Terry preference data, whereas math problems do not arrive as pairwise comparisons.
GRPO (from the DeepSeekMath paper) keeps the PPO update but deletes the value network, replacing the learned baseline with a z-score computed across a group of sampled rollouts for the same prompt. In the fully online case the clipping ratio is 1 and the clipping term does nothing, leaving advantage minus a KL penalty. The whole algorithm fits in about a page of code, which is why open-source work standardized on it.
GRPO is not the first-principles policy gradient. Dividing by the group standard deviation breaks the reinforce-with-baseline contract, which only permits subtracting a state-dependent baseline, and it upweights problems where reward variance is near zero — exactly the too-easy and too-hard cases. The per-token length normalization rewards long incorrect outputs, since dividing a negative reward by a longer sequence shrinks the penalty; Dr. GRPO’s plots show the famous growth in chain-of-thought length is driven by incorrect responses.
DeepSeek R1-Zero is the clean result: a base model plus GRPO with only accuracy and format rewards, no SFT, landing near OpenAI o1. Production R1 adds long chain-of-thought SFT, a language-consistency reward for interpretability, and a final RLHF stage. The viral “aha moment” and growing CoT length are less impressive than they appeared — the length growth follows from GRPO’s length normalization, and the aha phrasing already exists in the base model.
DeepSeek reported its failures, which is the useful part: process reward models that worked in DeepSeekMath were dropped for outcome-only supervision, and MCTS-style tree search did not work. Distilling R1’s chains of thought into Qwen 2.5 and Llama recovers much of the long-CoT ability by SFT alone, raising the open question of whether RL is needed as an algorithm or mainly as a source of supervision that nothing else can provide.
Kimi K1.5 reaches a GRPO-like update from a completely different DPO-style derivation, which suggests the group-mean baseline is the load-bearing component. It does not length-normalize, and instead adds an explicit length penalty to compress chains of thought — with the caveat that incorrect answers must not be compressed too aggressively or the model can never produce a long enough attempt to recover in a weak domain. Data work matters as much as the algorithm: best-of-8 filtering to keep problems in the solvable-but-not-solved band, and dropping problems once mastered.
Verifiability is leaky in practice. Math answer-equivalence checking ends up needing a regex or a reward model, so RLVR quietly reintroduces a reward model; the Lean compiler turns out not to be adversarially robust; and Qwen3-Coder-Next needed a dedicated reward to stop the agent reading future git commits, which had produced an emergent jump that was actually reward hacking. That run reached about 70.6% on SWE-bench with roughly three billion active parameters, though task-specific RL performance should not be assumed to generalize.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-17---Al.title: Stanford CS336 Lecture 17 - Alignment - Multimodality
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-17---Al.content:
Summary
Originally planned as more reinforcement learning, this lecture was reallocated to an overview of multimodal models on the grounds that the course would be incomplete without them. It traces the lineage from CLIP and SigLIP as image encoders, through the standard vision-language model template (encoder plus projector plus language model) as built by the LLaVA and Qwen series, and ends with Chameleon’s discrete-token alternative. The focus is almost entirely on the input side — how non-text data becomes something a transformer can consume — rather than on generation. The framing question throughout is what plays the role of the BPE tokenizer for images.
Key Takeaways

Transformers speak tokens, so every modality must be converted into discrete or continuous tokens where each token carries a semantic unit. A subword qualifies; a single pixel does not. Text tokenization is a mild annoyance, but for images there is no obvious equivalent.
CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder so that matched pairs have high dot products, which amounts to 2N softmax classification problems over a batch. It used 400 million scraped image-text pairs, a ViT-L/14 at 336x336 with attention pooling, and a GPT-2 style text encoder whose EOS activation represents the sequence. The headline result was that zero-shot CLIP beat a ResNet trained on 1.2 million annotated ImageNet images. Notably, training a stronger model to predict caption tokens did worse than bag-of-words CLIP for representation quality.
CLIP’s weaknesses are batch-related: it needs batches around 32,000, and the softmax spans the whole batch so it does not decompose the way language-model training does. SigLIP replaces the multi-class objective with a per-pair sigmoid — is this image and text aligned, yes or no — which decouples the loss from the batch size, permits a rotating shard schedule across devices to cover off-diagonal blocks, and trains far more cheaply (roughly five days on 32 TPUv4 versus ten days on 256 TPUv3).
The VLM template is to stitch, not to pretrain from scratch: a pretrained vision encoder, a projector into the language model’s embedding space, and a pretrained LM. LLaVA used CLIP ViT-L/14, a single linear matrix W, and Vicuna, trained in two stages — freeze everything and train W for alignment, then unfreeze the language model. Its 158,000 training examples were synthesized by prompting GPT-4 with human MS COCO captions and bounding boxes.
Fixed 336x336 crops destroy fine detail, which breaks OCR. AnyRes handles this by tiling an image into encoder-sized pieces plus one downsampled global view and concatenating the resulting vectors, interpolating down when there are too many. LLaVA-OneVision budgets tokens by modality: up to nine crops for a single image, base resolution for multiple images, and fewer tokens per frame for video with a cap around 32 frames.
Capability transfers across modality boundaries without matching training data. OCR trained only on single images supports multi-image GUI screenshot tasks, and visual prompting (circling a region) trained only on single images generalizes to tracking a highlighted player across video frames.
The Qwen line shows the adapter evolving: one layer of cross-attention to a fixed 256 tokens in Qwen-VL, then dynamic resolution with 2x2 patch merging and M-RoPE over height, width and time in Qwen2-VL, then in Qwen3-VL interleaving RoPE frequencies so every axis sees both low and high frequencies, explicit video timestamp tokens rather than implicit positional time, a square-root per-token loss normalization so long video examples do not dominate, and DeepStack, which injects vision embeddings directly into the language model’s residual stream instead of treating the encoder as a black box. Context reaches 256K, trained in stages of 8K, 32K and 256K.
Vision encoders stay under about a billion parameters while the language model can be 72 billion, because patch encoding is a local operation with little reasoning or knowledge in it; the capability lives in the language model.
Chameleon takes the opposite approach and discretizes images into tokens via a VQ-VAE, turning a 512x512 image into 1,024 tokens from an 8,000-entry codebook, so that text and images are generated by one ordinary language model with no adapter and interleaved output. It is elegant but was unstable, because image tokens have much higher entropy than text tokens and parameter norms grow; QK-norm and z-loss mitigated it. The approach lost ground because discretization destroys fine detail needed for OCR and diffusion became the better generation path. The lecturer’s speculation about frontier omni models is continuous encoders for understanding plus diffusion for generation.

sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-18---Gu.title: Stanford CS336 Guest Lecture - Dan Fu
sources/Stanford-CS336---Lecture-18---Gu.content:
Summary
A guest lecture on what happens after training: serving models, or turning electricity into tokens. The speaker, who runs a lab at UCSD and works at Together, walks through the lifetime of an inference request — scheduling, KV caching, prefill and decode, parallelism — then presents two research directions that come out of looking at the system closely. The first is megakernels, which fuse an entire model layer into a single GPU kernel to eliminate launch gaps and tail effects during decode. The second is Parcae, a looped or recurrent transformer stabilized using state-space model analysis. The argument tying it together is that deep understanding of inference and GPU kernels enables full-stack innovation in model design.
Key Takeaways

Prefill and decode are different beasts and are increasingly split across different machines. Prefill resembles training without the backward pass and is compute-bound; decode generates one token at a time, so it does little arithmetic but must reload the whole model, making it memory-bandwidth-bound. This asymmetry is driving hardware specialization, with vendors pairing GPUs for prefill against LPU-style chips such as Groq or Cerebras for decode.
Production traffic does not look like training data or like a made-up benchmark. A coding agent with a whole repository in context has tens of thousands of input tokens and short output; narrative summarization or casual chat look nothing like it. Session length, turn count, gaps between turns and per-application latency targets all shape what the serving system must optimize.
The KV cache hierarchy — GPU memory, then CPU DRAM, then SSD — recreates classic operating-system paging, down to LRU eviction being a decent heuristic and prefetching being the ideal if you could predict the next request. This is a concrete reason CPU performance and DRAM/SSD supply now matter to inference providers.
At trillions of tokens a day, failures that occur 0.001% of the time become routine. Examples given: a subtly wrong kernel producing NaN logits, after which the model repeats one token forever; a regression in tool-call handling that sent completion lengths into tens of thousands of tokens in a doom loop; and an off-by-one that read uninitialized GPU memory, emitting a random Chinese character that made the model switch languages — widely misdiagnosed as a quantization problem.
Cache-aware prefill-decode disaggregation is a two-line routing change with outsized payoff: send new, cold, low-cache-hit-rate requests to a dedicated set of prefill nodes so a freshly pasted book does not share GPUs with a user midway through a cheap conversation. Reported as up to 40% faster serving.
Megakernels attack the fact that writing one kernel per operation leaves the GPU idle during launch, teardown and tail effects. Fusing a whole layer into one kernel turns the GPU into a distributed system to be scheduled, allowing the KV cache load to begin before QKV and RoPE finish, or the output-projection weights to load before attention completes. This yields 30-70% speedups on the attention inference kernel and about 72% of achievable memory bandwidth on an H100, implemented via the ThunderKittens library.
The cost of megakernels is human: a talented kernel engineer spends roughly a year covering one hardware target, two or three models, and batch sizes 1 to 16 — change to batch size 17 and the work restarts. Compilers to automate this are in progress.
Parcae addresses why looped transformers blow up. Writing the residual as a dynamic system, pushing all the nonlinearity aside, leaves A and B matrices whose closed form is dominated by A raised to the number of loops; when the spectral radius exceeds 1 the activations explode, which explains loss spikes that previous work papered over by fixing the learning rate. Constraining A to a negative diagonal and normalizing B produces stable training at learning rates that broke baselines, plus better perplexity than both a prior recurrent-depth model and a strong transformer baseline.
Parcae’s scaling laws suggest recurrence is a third axis alongside parameters and data: at fixed parameters and FLOPs, the iso-curves trend down and to the right, implying recurrence should be scaled up as data increases. Since current production models use no recurrence at all, they sit at the far left of that curve. The serving payoff is that fewer parameters mean more room for KV cache and less cross-GPU communication.

Summary
Stanford CS336, “Language Modeling from Scratch”, Spring 2026 — the third edition of the course, taught by Percy Liang and Tatsunori Hashimoto with course assistants Marcel, Herman and Stephen. The premise is building a language model end to end rather than calling one: tokenization, architecture, kernels and hardware, distributed training, scaling laws, inference, data pipelines, and post-training. All 18 lectures are published on the Stanford Online YouTube channel, roughly 24 hours in total, recorded between 2026-04-14 and 2026-06-05.

sources/Steph-Ango---Notes-Thinking-Mode.title: Notes Thinking Model
sources/Steph-Ango---Notes-Thinking-Mode.content:
Source set:

stephango.com/vault
stephango.com/evergreen-notes
stephango.com/file-over-app
stephango.com/concise
stephango.com/style
